title: Understanding Their Feelings Isn't Enough
author: Growing Nurture
summary: The author of Growing Nurture, a teacher, former school leader and microschool founder writing as a mother, argues that gentle parenting has come to over-emphasise acknowledging children's feelings at the expense of teaching them what to do next. She opens with her own anxiety as a new mother and her questioning of the prevailing approach. Acknowledging a feeling, she says, is only the first step, and children also need chances to pause, reflect, weigh options and choose a response. She cites a 2020 meta-analysis linking childhood self-regulation to better achievement, relationships and health. She then offers five thinking skills she uses with children: noticing the body and using calming tools such as breathwork, separating feeling from fact, exploring why an emotion arose, understanding both sides of a story, and taking responsibility for mistakes. The piece is brief and personal, and closes by reminding parents that critical thinking guides emotions rather than opposing them.
points: Naming and validating a child's feelings is only the first half of emotional parenting; the second half is helping the child decide what to do with them.
A 2020 meta-analysis cited in the piece links childhood self-regulation to higher achievement, better interpersonal behaviour and better health.
Five thinking skills are offered: body awareness and calming, feeling versus fact, exploring the cause, seeing both sides, and owning mistakes.
Taking responsibility for mistakes is flagged as probably the hardest of the five, because blaming someone else is always easier.
The author frames critical thinking as a guide for emotions rather than their opposite, which gives parents a way to teach regulation without dismissing feeling.
quotes: I have heard parents say “I feel your feelings.” I understand the sentiment and I know it is often said with love, but acknowledging the feelings is only the first part.
We need to give them opportunities to pause, reflect on their thoughts, consider different options and decide the best way to respond.
Knowing they are understood is powerful, but helping them realise what to do next is the key to unlocking their potential. This is a skill, and one that we can nurture and build together.
A 2020 meta-analysis explored whether self-regulation in childhood relates to higher achievement, interpersonal behaviours and mental and physical health.
It found evidence that regulation in childhood is linked to better outcomes in all of those. So we can conclude, from the study, that self-regulation matters.
Knowing the difference between what we feel and what is fact. We may be feeling an emotion (like anger), but anger doesn’t define us.
Being aware of mistakes and taking responsibility. This may be one of the hardest skills to develop. It’s always easier to blame someone else.
And just a reminder that critical thinking is not the opposite of emotions, but a guide that stops emotions from ruling us.
